title: Set up Visual Studio 2019, the game's files and its first 3 classes
kind: a core chapter: every game you build later stands on chapters 2 to 10
one: You make your project in Visual Studio 2019 and put every picture, sound and data file where the game can find it. Then you add the 3 small classes that every game uses, and a menu bar.

stages.title: Get ready, and make the project

screens.title: See what this chapter makes, and the words it uses

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know what your project looks like at the end of this chapter.
Every later chapter adds to the project you make here. So this chapter sets up the things that every form and every game needs.
At the end of this chapter, your project has 5 things in it.

box.title: What you make in this chapter

blocks.p: A Windows Forms [[project|6]] called SummitReady, or your own game's name.
One window, frmLogin, with a menu bar along the top. Chapter 6 turns it into the log in window.
The Data, Images and Sounds folders, and `credits.txt`, in the [[bin\Debug|11]] folder.
3 small classes: Files finds files, Sound plays sounds, and Mix shuffles numbers.
A plan for your own pictures and sounds.

need: Your plan, with your topic and the forms you want (chapter 1).
A computer with Visual Studio 2019 on it (chapter 0).
About 2 hours. Your ticks are kept, so you can stop at the end of any screen and come back later.

words: Random
Gives numbers by chance. `random.Next` asks it for one whole number.
return
`return` hands a value back to the code that called the method, and ends the method there.
count up with ++
`++` adds 1 to a whole number. `i++` means i becomes one more than it was.
count down with --
`--` takes 1 away from a whole number. `i--` means i becomes one less than it was.
not
`!` in front of a true or false value turns it the other way. `!File.Exists(path)` is true when the file is missing.
random number
A whole number picked by chance. `random.Next(i + 1)` gives one from 0 up to i.
project
Everything Visual Studio 2019 needs to build one program: its forms, its classes and its settings.
file name extension
The letters after the last dot in a file's name, such as `.txt` or `.zip`. They tell you what kind of file it is.
form
A window in your program. Visual Studio 2019 shows a form in the designer, where you drag controls onto it.
Solution Explorer
The list on the right of Visual Studio 2019 that shows every file in your project.
Properties window
The list under Solution Explorer that shows the settings of whatever you have clicked.
bin\Debug
The folder inside your project where Visual Studio 2019 puts the program it builds. Summit Ready reads its data, pictures and sounds from there.
zip file
One file with other files and folders packed inside it.
build
Visual Studio 2019 turns your code into a program you can run. If any line is wrong, the build stops and lists the error.
class
A named group of methods and values, kept in its own `.cs` file.
static
A `static` class or method belongs to the class itself, so every form shares one copy. You use it by writing the class name, as in `Files.Data("kit.txt")`.
method
A named set of lines that does one job. Code runs the lines by writing the method's name.
Path.Combine
Joins folder names and a file name into one path (the full address of a file), with the right slashes between them.
null
Nothing at all. `Picture` gives back `null` when the picture file is missing.
field
A named box that holds a value, written at the top of the class, outside every method. Every method in the class can use it.
bool
A value that is only ever true or false. `Muted` is a `bool`.
or
`||` means or. The `if` is true when any one of its parts is true.
array
A row of values of the same type, kept together under one name and numbered from 0. `numbers[0]` is the first number.
switch
Picks one `case` to run, by the value in its brackets. `default` runs when no case matches.
MenuStrip
A control that puts a menu bar along the top of a form, such as File and Help.
event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click on a menu item.
event handler
The method that runs when something happens to a control, such as a click on a menu item. `mnuExit_Click` runs when the player clicks Exit.
sender
Every event handler is given `sender`: the control that the event happened to.
MessageBox
A small window with a message and an OK button. `MessageBox.Show` opens one.
licence
The rules that say how you may use a picture or a sound that somebody else made.
red underline
The wavy red line Visual Studio 2019 draws under code it does not understand yet.
blocks.intro: You do not need to learn these words now. Where you first meet each one in the chapter, it has a dotted line under it. Hover over it or tap it to see what it means.

blocks.p: Now set the form's settings in the Properties window, using the table below. Set **Font** first, because changing Font later makes Visual Studio 2019 resize the form. Set **FormBorderStyle** before **Size** for the same reason.
Click the box beside the property's name in the Properties window. Type the new value, then press Enter.
For **Font**, click the box beside Font, then click the small button with 3 dots at the right of the box. Pick Segoe UI and size 11, then click **OK**.
For **BackColor**, type `243, 245, 242` in the box beside BackColor, then press Enter.
For **StartPosition**, **FormBorderStyle** and **MaximizeBox**, click the arrow at the right of the box, then click the value in the list.

FixedSingle and MaximizeBox = False stop the player making the window bigger. Every Summit Ready window is 1000 by 660 inside its border, so nothing on it can be pushed out of place. Size = 1016, 699 is a little bigger, because it counts the border and the title bar too.

blocks.p: **Data** holds the text files. Each line of a text file is one thing, such as one player or one knot, with a bar `|` between its parts. Chapter 3 reads the first one, `players.txt`.
**Images** holds the pictures, in one folder for each kind of picture. The 8 avatars are in Avatars, and the 8 knot photos are in Knots.
**Sounds** holds every sound, as a `.wav` file.
`credits.txt` says who made each picture and sound, and the [[licence|29]] that lets you use it. Stage 5 of this chapter shows you how to read it.

Every name is in small letters, with the kind of thing first, such as `avatar-fox.png` and `knot-bowline.jpg`. Name your own files the same way, so you can always tell what a file holds from its name.
Never put a file anywhere else. The code looks only in these 3 folders.

code.title: Files.cs: the Files class
partLines: The class
The comment says what the class is for. `static` means every form shares one copy, so you never make your own. You call its methods on the class name, as in `Files.Data("players.txt")`.
Data

`Application.StartupPath` is the folder the program runs from, which is bin\Debug. `Path.Combine` joins folder names with the right slashes. So `Files.Data("players.txt")` gives the full path to `players.txt` in the Data folder.
Image
Image does the same for a picture, but it also needs the folder inside Images, such as Avatars. The line is long, so it carries on onto a second line. C# reads the 2 lines as one, up to the `;`.
Sound
Sound gives the full path to a sound in the Sounds folder.
Picture

Picture loads a picture so a form can show it. First it finds the path with Image. If the file is not there, it gives back `null`, which means nothing, so the game shows no picture and carries on. Otherwise `Image.FromFile` loads the picture.

code.title: Sound.cs: the Sound class
partLines: The class
Sound is `static`, like Files, so every form shares one Sound class.
The 2 fields

A [[field|19]] is a variable at the top of the class, outside every method. `Muted` is true when the player has turned the sound off. Every form can read it and change it. `player` is the one SoundPlayer that plays every sound.
Find the sound, or stop
`Files.Sound` gives the full path to the sound. If the sound is muted, or the file is not there, `return` stops the method, so nothing plays and nothing crashes.
Play it
`SoundLocation` tells the SoundPlayer which file to play. `Play` starts it. A new sound stops any sound that is still playing.

code.title: Mix.cs: the Mix class and ShuffledNumbers
partLines: The class and its Random
`random` is a [[field|19]] that makes random numbers. The class keeps only one, so two shuffles close together never give the same order.
Start with the numbers in order
`int[]` is an [[array|22]]: a row of whole numbers, numbered from 0. The first loop, a few lines that repeat, fills it with 0, 1, 2 and so on, up to `count - 1`.
Shuffle them

The second loop starts at the last number and works back to the front. `random.Next(i + 1)` picks a place `j` from 0 to `i`. The 3 lines after it swap the numbers in places `i` and `j`. `keep` holds one number while the other one moves.
Hand them back
`return numbers;` hands the shuffled numbers back. `Mix.ShuffledNumbers(4)` might give 2, 0, 3, 1.

screens.title: Read credits.txt, the list of who made each picture and sound

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know what each part of a line in `credits.txt` means.
Every picture and sound in Summit Ready was made by somebody else. Each one has a [[licence|29]] that lets you use it, as long as you say who made it. Saying so is called a credit.
`credits.txt` holds one line for each picture and sound. These are its heading line and 3 of its credits.

code.title: credits.txt: the heading line and 3 of its credits
code.text:
file|what it shows|who made it|licence|where it came from
avatar-badger.png|badger [1F9A1]|OpenMoji (HfG Schwäbisch Gmünd)|CC BY-SA 4.0|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hfg-gmuend/openmoji/master/color/618x618/1F9A1.png
click.wav|button click|Kenney (kenney.nl)|CC0 1.0|https://kenney.nl/assets/ui-audio

partLines: The heading line
The first line names the 5 parts. Like every data file, the parts have a bar `|` between them.
A picture
The file name, what it shows, who made it, its licence, and the web page it came from. OpenMoji made the badger. CC BY-SA 4.0 means you may use it if you credit OpenMoji.
A sound
Kenney made the click. CC0 means anyone may use it for anything, but you still credit it.
A photo
The bowline photo comes from Wikimedia Commons. Its page there names the person who took it, and the licence.

blocks.p: The licences you may use are CC0, CC BY, CC BY-SA and public domain. A picture or sound with any other licence, or with no licence, stays out of your game.

screens.title: Find your own pictures and sounds, and add a credit for each one

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know where to find pictures and sounds you may use, and how to credit them.
Your game is on your own topic, so it needs some pictures and sounds of its own. These 3 websites have thousands, and every one has a licence you may use.
**OpenMoji**, at openmoji.org, has bright emoji pictures. They make good avatars (small pictures that stand for a player) and icons. Every picture is CC BY-SA 4.0, and its page shows its code number.
**Wikimedia Commons**, at commons.wikimedia.org, has photos of almost anything: places, animals, elements, buildings. Each photo's page names its author and its licence, under Licensing.
**Kenney**, at kenney.nl, has game sounds and game pictures. Everything there is CC0.

Pictures are `.png` or `.jpg` files. Sounds are `.wav` files, because the game's sound player, SoundPlayer, plays only `.wav`. If a sound ends in `.mp3` or `.ogg`, look for another sound that ends in `.wav`. Changing the end of the file name does not work.
Name each file in small letters, with its kind first and no spaces, such as `avatar-otter.png`.
Put each picture in the right folder inside bin\Debug\Images, and each sound in bin\Debug\Sounds.
Add a line to `credits.txt` for each file, with the 5 parts in the same order as the other lines.
Keep the web page address of every file as you download it. You need it for the credit.
A credit line for your own otter avatar from OpenMoji looks like this one.

code.title: A credit line for your own picture
partLines: One credit line
The file name, what it shows, who made it, the licence, and the web page. Type a bar `|` with Shift and the key to the left of Z.

blocks.p: To add a line, right-click `credits.txt` in bin\Debug and choose Open with, then Notepad. Click at the end of the last line, press Enter, and type your line. Press Ctrl and S together to save.
Your own files go in later, as you build each game. Make a list now of the pictures and sounds your plan needs, and the website where you will look for each one.

glossary: Random
Gives numbers by chance. `random.Next` asks it for one whole number.
return
`return` hands a value back to the code that called the method, and ends the method there.
count up with ++
`++` adds 1 to a whole number. `i++` means i becomes one more than it was.
count down with --
`--` takes 1 away from a whole number. `i--` means i becomes one less than it was.
not
`!` in front of a true or false value turns it the other way. `!File.Exists(path)` is true when the file is missing.
random number
A whole number picked by chance. `random.Next(i + 1)` gives one from 0 up to i.
project
Everything Visual Studio 2019 needs to build one program: its forms, its classes and its settings.
file name extension
The letters after the last dot in a file's name, such as `.txt` or `.zip`. They tell you what kind of file it is.
form
A window in your program. Visual Studio 2019 shows a form in the designer, where you drag controls onto it.
Solution Explorer
The list on the right of Visual Studio 2019 that shows every file in your project.
Properties window
The list under Solution Explorer that shows the settings of whatever you have clicked.
bin\Debug
The folder inside your project where Visual Studio 2019 puts the program it builds. Summit Ready reads its data, pictures and sounds from there.
zip file
One file with other files and folders packed inside it.
build
Visual Studio 2019 turns your code into a program you can run. If any line is wrong, the build stops and lists the error.
class
A named group of methods and values, kept in its own `.cs` file.
static
A `static` class or method belongs to the class itself, so every form shares one copy. You use it by writing the class name, as in `Files.Data("kit.txt")`.
method
A named set of lines that does one job. Code runs the lines by writing the method's name.
Path.Combine
Joins folder names and a file name into one path (the full address of a file), with the right slashes between them.
null
Nothing at all. `Picture` gives back `null` when the picture file is missing.
field
A named box that holds a value, written at the top of the class, outside every method. Every method in the class can use it.
bool
A value that is only ever true or false. `Muted` is a `bool`.
or
`||` means or. The `if` is true when any one of its parts is true.
array
A row of values of the same type, kept together under one name and numbered from 0. `numbers[0]` is the first number.
switch
Picks one `case` to run, by the value in its brackets. `default` runs when no case matches.
MenuStrip
A control that puts a menu bar along the top of a form, such as File and Help.
event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click on a menu item.
event handler
The method that runs when something happens to a control, such as a click on a menu item. `mnuExit_Click` runs when the player clicks Exit.
sender
Every event handler is given `sender`: the control that the event happened to.
MessageBox
A small window with a message and an OK button. `MessageBox.Show` opens one.
licence
The rules that say how you may use a picture or a sound that somebody else made.
red underline
The wavy red line Visual Studio 2019 draws under code it does not understand yet.
